extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology / literary analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and classify narrative levels and modes of reported speech (direct, indirect, free indirect, narrator's text) and analyze relations between primary and embedded texts in prose narrative. Includes signals, diagnostic tests, and functional effects (foreshadowing, mirror-text, immersion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal vs impersonal language situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish two language situations in a narrative text: a personal language situation (language about contact between speaker and hearer) and an impersonal language situation (language about others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals that indicate which language situation is operating include pronouns, grammatical person, tense, deixis, emotive/conative features, and modal expressions. The text gives a diagnostic table: personal: I/you; first and second person; not all past tenses are possible; deictic pronouns this/these, here/there, adverbs of place; today/tomorrow adverbs of time; emotive words/aspects (oh!); conative words/aspects (please, address, command, question); modal verbs/adverbs indicating uncertainty in the speaker (perhaps). Impersonal: he/she; third person; all past tenses; that/those; in that place; that day/the day after; emotive/conative/modal markers often absent. Use these signals to determine whether a passage expresses the standpoint of a narrator or of an actor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of perceptible narrator (NI(p)), CN2 (dramatic), and text interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify instances where personal-language signals refer to (a) the narrator (perceptible narrator NI(p)), (b) actors on a second narrative level with explicit level-change markers (CN2/dramatic), or (c) when personal language intrudes without explicit level change (text interference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If personal signals refer to the narrator = NI(p). If signals refer to actors and a clear change of level is indicated by a declarative verb, colon, dash, or quotation marks = CN2 (dramatic; actors communicate as on stage). If actors participate without stepping down from their narrative level (no explicit level change) then narrative levels intertwine or merge = text interference. Note the inverse possibility: actors' words may be represented at the narrator's level so that the narrator adopts the actor's discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics that define indirect discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect discourse is defined by three characteristics that distinguish it from direct speech and other modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three characteristics listed are: (1) Indirect discourse is narrated at a higher level than the level at which the words in the fabula are supposed to have been spoken. (2) The narrator’s text explicitly indicates that the words of an actor are narrated by means of a declarative verb and a conjunction, or a substitute for it. (3) The words of the actor appear to have been rendered with maximum precision and elaboration. Use these characteristics jointly to identify indirect discourse; each characteristic helps discriminate indirect discourse from direct speech, FID, and narrator’s text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and diagnostics of free indirect discourse (FID)
rubrics_metrics.description: FID (free indirect discourse / free indirect style / reported discourse) is a mixture/interference between narrator’s text and actor’s text: characteristic (2) of indirect discourse (explicit marker) is absent while characteristic (3) (presence of actor-style features) is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the explicit indicator (declarative verb + conjunction) is missing, FID is not always clear-cut. Only distinguish FID from ordinary narrator’s text when there are positive indications of representation of actor speech. Positive indications include: (1) signals of a personal language situation referring to an actor, (2) a strikingly personal style attributable to an actor, (3) more details about what has been said than is necessary for the course of the fabula. Examples (Elizabeth/John series) illustrate gradations: some forms (o.i, o.ii) show stronger or weaker FID. Treat identification as relative and context-sensitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signals indicating representation of an actor’s words
rubrics_metrics.description: List of observable textual signs that suggest the narrator is representing an actor's utterance (directly, indirectly, or freely-indirectly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key signals: presence of personal deictics (tomorrow, might), modal markings tied to the actor's subjectivity, change of person pronoun (I → she), shifts in tense (present future → past future), stylistic markers attributable to a character, deictic adjuncts (like this), emotive or conative particles. Use these to argue that a passage encodes actor speech rather than plain narrator summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuum of representation: direct → indirect → free indirect → narrator’s text
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative modes form a continuum in which fidelity to an actor’s original words decreases while the representation of speaking as an act (narratorial summarizing) increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct speech preserves the exact wording (highest fidelity). Indirect discourse reports the content at a higher level with explicit markers. Free indirect discourse mixes actor and narrator signals without explicit markers and occupies a middle position. Narrator’s text treats speaking primarily as an act and often omits textual representation of words. In analysis, assess degree and proportion: sometimes actor’s text dominates, sometimes narrator’s text dominates; the degree is relative and can vary even within a passage (see examples m–p).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic procedure for disentangling interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical guidance for teasing apart narrator’s discourse, direct/indirect discourse, and FID in passages where they intermingle (e.g., Flaubert).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for verbs of saying, quotation punctuation, changes in grammatical person and tense, deictic elements ('tomorrow', 'like this'), emotive and conative markers, and stylistic idiosyncrasies attributable to characters. Track which signals point to narrator vs actor. Note that some transitions may be seamless or deliberate to create immersion; be cautious about attributing sections to one level without multiple converging signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of dependence and hierarchy between primary narrator’s text and embedded actor’s text
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrator’s text is considered 'primary' and embedded actor’s texts subordinate; the connection is hierarchical (level-based) and can vary in kind and intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the dependence of actor’s text on narrator’s text like the relation of a subordinate clause to a main clause. Quantitative aspects matter: the more sentences that frame the actor’s text, the stronger the dependence. The formal hierarchy does not imply qualitative value; instead it marks level relations for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of embedded fabulae: explanatory, transformative, or minimal
rubrics_metrics.description: Embedded stories (embedded fabulae) can function to explain the primary fabula, to resemble/mirror it, to transform the primary fabula (influence outcomes), or be minimal/declarative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the embedded text explains the primary situation, it may dominate reader attention and be more important than the primary fabula. If it resembles the primary fabula (mirror-text), it may foreshadow or retrospectively inflect meaning. Embedded texts may also be minimal (a single declarative embedded sentence) with limited function. Evaluate the degree to which the embedded fabula influences or explains the primary fabula (examples: cautionary tale structure vs Beloved vs Arabian Nights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mirror-text (resemblance) detection and interpretive effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Define and detect when an embedded fabula resembles the primary fabula (mirror-text) and describe its interpretive roles (foreshadowing, prefiguring, retrospective significance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational test: paraphrase both fabulas; if the paraphrases share one or more striking elements, treat the embedded text as resembling the primary. Degree of resemblance is measured by how many terms/schematic elements the paraphrases share. Placement matters: mirror-texts near the beginning can predict endings (veiled to preserve suspense); near the end they provide retrospective significance and lift the narration to a more general level (e.g., Kafka). Beware that resemblance is never identity; interpretive functions include prefiguring, signaling how to read, and altering suspense dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of embedded/mirror-text and effects for reader and actor
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an embedded or mirror-text appears in the primary narrative shapes its effect on readers and, potentially, on characters who interpret it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an embedded mirror-text occurs early, it may foreshadow the outcome (reducing suspense unless resemblance is veiled). If it occurs late, it tends to be retrospective, enhancing significance. The embedded text may also serve as an 'indication to the actor'—a character who discerns the mirror relation can use it to alter their fate (example: Poe's 'The Fall of the House of Usher' where a character reads a double-meaning embedded text and escapes). Consider both reader- and character-facing interpretive consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-narrative embedded texts and the dramatic effect of dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Many embedded texts are non-narrative (assertions, discussions, descriptions, confidences), with dialogue being the predominant non-narrative form; extensive embedded dialogue increases the dramatic quality of a narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat embedded dialogues as dramatic episodes: because speakers themselves produce meaning through interaction, the more dialogue a narrative contains, the more the narrative approximates a dramatic text. Use the proportion of dialogue and its internal coherence to assess how 'dramatic' a narrative section is relative to purely narrator-driven exposition.
